title: Gdje je Mostar?
theme: Map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mostar tease

vocabulary.example: Mostar je u Bosni i Hercegovini.

grammar.title: Gdje je…?
grammar.explanation: Gdje? Means where. Pair it with je for a ready question. Ask Gdje je Mostar? Ask Gdje je mapa? Ask Gdje je Amira?

grammar.title: Ovdje and tamo
grammar.explanation: Ovdje means here, near you. Tamo means there or over there, farther away. On a map Emir points and says Sarajevo je ovdje. He says Mostar je tamo. Practice with your finger on the page.

grammar.title: U / na / kod. Ready place lines
grammar.explanation: Learn these place lines whole rather than building them word by word. U Sarajevu = in Sarajevo. Na mapi = on the map. Kod Amire = at Amira’s. Na jugu = in the south. The grammar behind each ending can wait.

culture.title: Finding Mostar on a real map
culture.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina stretches from green hills to the Neretva valley. Sarajevo sits in a mountain bowl. Mostar lies farther south and is famous for Stari Most, the Old Bridge over the cold Neretva. Emir does not spoil the ending of Book 1. Today Ana only finds Mostar on the map, asks Gdje je Mostar?, and hears the answer Tamo. The trip can wait. The map habit starts now.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Gdje / ovdje / tamo
lessonBlocks.body: Ask Gdje je…? About anything on the table, such as mapa, kahva, or Mrvica. Answer Ovdje! When it is near. Answer Tamo! When you point away. Add city names. Ask Gdje je Sarajevo? And answer Ovdje. Ask Gdje je Mostar? And answer Tamo. Drill ten times with a finger on an imaginary map. Emir makes Ana point south for Mostar every time she asks.
tips: Ask with Gdje je plus a place.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. On the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina
lessonBlocks.body: Open the map. Say Na mapi. Find Sarajevo and say U Sarajevu. Add ovdje. Find Mostar and say Mostar je tamo, na jugu. Name the river and bridge as story bait. Say Neretva je rijeka. Say Stari most. Then place yourselves. Say Mi smo kod Amire, u Sarajevu. Emir grins and says Mostar? Uskoro. Ana writes Gdje je Mostar? In her notebook and draws a tiny bridge.
tips: Keep u Sarajevu, na mapi, kod Amire, and na jugu ready.

funFacts.title: Mostar means the bridge keeper
funFacts.body: Mostar’s name is tied to the bridge and the people who kept the crossing. The root links to most, the word for bridge. Stari Most is the famous postcard, but the whole old town carries the story. Remember the name’s meaning when you pin Mostar on the map in this lesson.

funFacts.title: Ovdje vs tamo
funFacts.body: Bosnian learners often mix ovdje and tamo. Ovdje means here, and tamo means there. A simple hand habit helps keep them straight, with your palm down for ovdje and a point away for tamo. Practice the pair out loud until the gestures and words stay attached.

funFacts.title: Kod plus a name
funFacts.body: Kod Amire is how you say you are at Amira’s place. Bosnian uses kod plus a person for homes, shops, and cafés all the time. It is shorter and more natural than building a full address every visit. Learn the pattern now, because you will reuse it for almost every friendly destination.

funFacts.title: The Mostar trip can wait
funFacts.body: Book 1 saves the real Mostar trip for later on purpose. Lesson 5 only marks Mostar on the map and practices the question Gdje je Mostar? Emir’s grin hints that the trip is coming, but not yet. For today, find the city on the map and let the visit wait.

civicContext.title: Mostar went twelve years without local elections
civicContext.body: Mostar is a map lesson and a civic warning at the same time. Disputes over ethnically engineered election rules left the city without local elections from 2008 to 2020. Ordinary municipal democracy froze while courts and politicians fought over power-sharing formulas. Asking where Mostar is on the map also means remembering that postwar rules can stop a city from voting for more than a decade.
